input.utterance: I'm updating our safeguarding card for a resident-money discrepancy. Who receives the first escalation now, what part does Finance keep, and which current role name and outside-agency sharing route should the card use?

displayed_text:
Escalate the discrepancy to the Alderbridge Safeguarding Lead as the first contact — the policy replaces the previous Finance Manager-first route and requires immediate escalation to the Safeguarding Lead for a financial concern.

Finance retains responsibility for the financial-record and audit aspects: the Finance Manager is brought in to support the financial record review once the Safeguarding Lead has taken the concern forward, and resident fund transaction records, appointeeship files and audit findings are kept per the Records Retention Schedule; the Finance Manager also audits resident fund records quarterly.

Use the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead as the role name on the card for internal escalation, and include the external agency sharing routes now specified for financial abuse concerns — namely referral routes to the Office of the Public Guardian (where an attorney or deputy may be acting outside their authority) and to Action Fraud (for suspected fraud or scam); also retain the local authority safeguarding team referral route where the local threshold is met.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the Adult Safeguarding Policy (the framework a financial concern now
escalates directly into) and the Records Retention Schedule (governing how long financial records are
kept).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the new escalation route. A staff member notices a resident's personal
allowance balance is lower than the transaction record suggests it should be. They report this to the
registered manager the same day, who escalates it directly to the Alderbridge Safeguarding Lead as a
financial concern, with the Finance Manager then brought in to support the financial record review rather
than receiving the initial escalation as under the previous version.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was the escalation contact changed to the Safeguarding Lead?** A review found routing a financial
concern through the Finance Manager first sometimes delayed the safeguarding assessment that
ultimately mattered most; escalating directly to the Safeguarding Lead removes that delay. **Does the
Finance Manager still have a role?** Yes, they support the financial record and audit aspect once the
Safeguarding Lead has taken the concern forward, but no longer receive the initial escalation.

Training and competency

Staff handling resident funds complete financial safeguarding training at induction, refreshed annually,
updated to reflect the Safeguarding Lead as the escalation contact for a financial concern.

Monitoring and compliance

The Alderbridge Finance Manager audits resident fund records quarterly across every site, with
financial-concern-specific findings now also reported through the Safeguarding Lead's own quarterly
safeguarding report to the Board.

Record keeping and retention

Resident fund transaction records, appointeeship files and audit findings are retained per the Records
Retention Schedule.

Approval and review history

This policy was originally approved by the Chief Executive on 1 March 2025 and this version took effect 1
March 2026, superseding the earlier version.

Resident Finances and Appointeeship Policy

Supersedes the version effective 1 March 2025. Changes the escalation contact for a financial concern
from the Alderbridge Finance Manager to the Alderbridge Safeguarding Lead, reflecting that a financial
concern is treated primarily as a safeguarding matter.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds
or acting under a financial authority on a resident's behalf.

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy is the umbrella safeguarding document; several other documents govern specific
safeguarding-adjacent situations and are not restated here. The Allegations Against Staff Procedure
governs the parallel process that runs where the person alleged to have caused harm is a member of staff.
The Missing Person Procedure governs the specific immediate-search and police-contact steps where a

assessed for the specific decision at hand, referenced throughout this policy rather than duplicated. The
Resident Finances and Appointeeship Policy governs financial-abuse-adjacent concerns arising from how
a resident's own money is handled. The Whistleblowing Policy provides an alternative external route for a
member of staff who does not feel able to raise a concern through this policy's normal internal route.

duty. Willow Bank Community Service's safeguarding champion additionally maintains a log of any

appears to have been shared beyond the people who should hold it), reflecting the specific risk profile of

This overarching policy sits above the full safeguarding policy suite and now explicitly incorporates the multi-agency information sharing principles previously handled inconsistently on a case-by-case basis.

Why self-neglect was added

A review found staff were unsure how to respond when a resident with capacity chose to live in a way that raised health or safety concerns, such as declining support with personal care to a degree affecting their wellbeing; the new Self-Neglect Guidance gives a clear, respectful framework balancing a resident's autonomy against a genuine duty of care.

Why terminology was aligned to Safeguarding Champion

Following the site-level role's rename from 'safeguarding lead' to 'Safeguarding Champion', this overarching document's own references were inconsistent with the current title; this version aligns terminology throughout to avoid a reader being confused about whether 'safeguarding lead' meant the site role or the organisation-level role, which retains a distinct title.

Safeguarding Adults Board engagement

Alderbridge participates in the relevant local authority's Safeguarding Adults Board where a site's residents fall within that authority's area, contributing to multi-agency learning and receiving updates on local safeguarding priorities; the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead represents Alderbridge at this Board.

The role of an advocate

Where a resident lacks capacity to fully participate in a safeguarding process, or would benefit from independent support regardless of capacity, an independent advocate is arranged to represent the resident's own wishes and interests throughout the process, distinct from a family member's role.

Whole-suite training pathway

Direct care staff	Level 2	Every 3 years

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. Self-neglect's formal addition in this version continues that same pattern.

The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. A self-neglect situation, in particular, calls empowerment and proportionality sharply into focus, since respecting a capacitous resident's own choice while still exercising a genuine duty of care requires balancing these principles carefully rather than defaulting reflexively to either extreme.

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Wherever a resident is able to participate, their own wishes and views are sought and given real weight throughout a safeguarding process, not merely noted as a formality; this is especially central to a self-neglect situation, where the resident's own account of their choices and priorities is the starting point for any supportive response.

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Where a resident's safeguarding history involves a local authority area outside where their current Alderbridge site sits, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead liaises with the originating authority to ensure relevant history transfers appropriately, using the multi-agency information sharing principles this version formalises.

Learning from a serious case review

Where Alderbridge is involved in, or a sector-wide serious case review identifies a lesson relevant to, a serious safeguarding failure, the Safeguarding Lead ensures that lesson is considered against this overarching policy and its suite, with any resulting change tracked and communicated to staff.

Supporting a staff member involved in a difficult safeguarding case

A staff member closely involved in a distressing safeguarding case, whether as the person who raised the concern or as part of the response, is offered support similar to that available following a resident's death, recognising that safeguarding work, including a self-neglect case that can be particularly difficult to sit with, is emotionally demanding even when handled well.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

meeting to address.

Confidentiality and Alderbridge's duty of candour

an active multi-agency safeguarding process, including one involving a financial abuse investigation; the
registered manager seeks guidance from the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead on what can honestly
and appropriately be said at that stage.

Working with an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate

Where a resident lacks capacity to make a specific decision relevant to a multi-agency safeguarding
process, including a financial decision under investigation by the Office of the Public Guardian, and has no
appropriate family member or friend to consult, an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate is instructed per
the Mental Capacity Act's own specific provisions.

Safeguarding considerations during transport or transfer

Where a resident's participation in a multi-agency process requires transport, such as attending an
interview connected to a financial abuse investigation, the arrangement itself considers the resident's
dignity, any mobility or clinical need, and whether a familiar member of staff should accompany them.

Purpose and scope

This protocol sets out how Alderbridge Care Group works with external agencies to protect a resident from
harm, now explicitly including the agency routes relevant to a financial abuse concern. It applies to every
site and every member of staff.

Policy statement

A safeguarding concern is rarely resolved by Alderbridge acting alone; effective safeguarding depends on
genuine, well-coordinated partnership with external agencies, now explicitly including the Office of the
Public Guardian and Action Fraud for a financial abuse concern, aligning this protocol with the
Safeguarding Policy (Overarching)'s own formal recognition of financial abuse within its suite.

Definitions

**LADO** the Local Authority Designated Officer. **Safeguarding Adults Board (SAB)** the statutory
multi-agency board. **Regional manager liaison role** the coordination function supporting a multi-site or
complex concern. **Office of the Public Guardian** the new external agency route, introduced in this
version, with statutory powers to investigate a concern about an attorney or deputy acting outside their
proper authority. **Action Fraud** the new external route, introduced in this version, for reporting a
suspected fraud against a resident.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any member of staff** reports a safeguarding concern to the registered manager immediately. **The
registered manager** makes the initial external referral decision, now including a financial abuse concern's
specific new routes where relevant. **The organisation-level Safeguarding Lead** coordinates the most
complex situations, including a financial abuse concern requiring Office of the Public Guardian or Action
Fraud involvement, and attends the local Safeguarding Adults Board.

Why the financial abuse agency routes were added

Following the Safeguarding Policy (Overarching)'s own formal recognition of financial abuse within its
suite, a review found this protocol's external agency list did not yet reflect the specific agencies relevant to
a financial abuse concern beyond the local authority safeguarding team itself; the Office of the Public
Guardian and Action Fraud routes close that gap, giving staff and the Safeguarding Lead a complete
picture of where a financial abuse concern might appropriately be referred.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the new routes. A concern arises that a resident's attorney has been making
financial decisions inconsistent with the resident's own known wishes and apparent best interests. The
organisation-level Safeguarding Lead refers to the local authority safeguarding team per the standard
route, and separately refers to the Office of the Public Guardian given its specific statutory power to
investigate and, where necessary, remove an attorney acting outside their proper authority, illustrating how
the two referrals complement rather than duplicate each other.

Frequently asked questions

**Does a financial abuse concern always need referring to both the local authority and one of the new
specific agencies?** Not always; the Safeguarding Lead assesses which agency or combination is
genuinely relevant to the specific concern, though a serious concern often benefits from more than one
route being pursued. **Why is Action Fraud relevant to a care home resident?** An older or vulnerable
resident is sometimes specifically targeted by a scam or fraud, including one involving a caller
impersonating a trusted organisation; Action Fraud is the appropriate national reporting route for this kind
of crime specifically.

Information sharing principles

Extended worked example: a financial concern

A worked example illustrates a financial abuse concern, a category staff have told the Safeguarding Lead
they find harder to recognise than physical harm. A care worker at Meadow Court notices that a resident's
small personal spending allowance, usually £20 a week and tracked in the individual resident finance
ledger under the Resident Finances and Appointeeship Policy, has been withdrawn in full every week for

concern is reported to the registered manager the same day, who reviews the ledger, finds no explanation

often only visible as a pattern over time.

Resident and family involvement in medication decisions

Wherever a resident has capacity, they are involved directly in decisions about their own medication; where capacity is lacking, family or an advocate is involved in a best-interests process rather than a purely clinical decision being made without any input beyond the care team itself.

Medication reconciliation on admission and transfer

Every resident's full medication list is reconciled against the prescribing GP's own record at admission, and again at any hospital transfer in either direction, since a mismatch between what a resident is believed to be taking and what they are actually prescribed is one of the most common sources of a serious medication error. This reconciliation is completed by a registered nurse or the registered manager, never left solely to an informal handover conversation.

Managing a medication change communicated verbally

Where a GP communicates a medication change verbally, this is confirmed in writing before the change is actually implemented, except in a genuine emergency where immediate action is clinically necessary; a verbal instruction alone is not treated as sufficient authority for an ongoing change to a resident's regular medication regimen.

End of life medication considerations

Medication management at the end of a resident's life often involves a different balance of priorities than routine administration, with comfort and symptom control given particular weight consistent with the End of Life Care Policy; this overarching document's core principles still apply in full, adapted to that different clinical context.

Moving to a new home is a big change, and staff pay particular attention to how a new resident is settling in during their first few weeks, checking in regularly and adjusting their care plan as staff get to know their preferences better.

Health appointments and clinical support

A resident's GP, dentist, optician and any other health appointment is arranged and supported by staff, who accompany a resident who wants company, and keep the family informed of anything significant, with the resident's own consent.

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Wherever a resident is able to participate, their own wishes and views are sought and given real weight throughout a safeguarding process, not merely noted as a formality; this is especially central to a self-neglect situation, where the resident's own account of their choices and priorities is the starting point for any supportive response.

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Where a resident's safeguarding history involves a local authority area outside where their current Alderbridge site sits, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead liaises with the originating authority to ensure relevant history transfers appropriately, using the multi-agency information sharing principles this version formalises.

Learning from a serious case review

Where Alderbridge is involved in, or a sector-wide serious case review identifies a lesson relevant to, a serious safeguarding failure, the Safeguarding Lead ensures that lesson is considered against this overarching policy and its suite, with any resulting change tracked and communicated to staff.

Supporting a staff member involved in a difficult safeguarding case

A staff member closely involved in a distressing safeguarding case, whether as the person who raised the concern or as part of the response, is offered support similar to that available following a resident's death, recognising that safeguarding work, including a self-neglect case that can be particularly difficult to sit with, is emotionally demanding even when handled well.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the escalation expected when a specified technique no longer seems right. A care worker at Meadow Court is due to assist a resident using a standing hoist per their MHRA, but on the day finds the resident notably weaker and less able to bear any weight than described in the assessment. Frequently asked questions

**What if a resident refuses to be hoisted and insists they can walk?** Their view is listened to and respected as far as safely possible, but staff do not abandon the specified technique based on the resident's own view of their capability alone; where this becomes a recurring tension, the MHRA is reviewed with the resident's involvement to find an approach that respects their autonomy while remaining genuinely safe. **Can an agency worker use equipment they've never used at Alderbridge before, if they say they're experienced with a similar model?** No — every member of staff, however experienced elsewhere, is assessed on Alderbridge's own specific equipment before using it unsupervised. **What if the specified sling size doesn't seem to fit properly?** Do not proceed with an ill-fitting sling; use an alternative in the correct size and report the mismatch so stock levels or the MHRA's own sling-size specification can be corrected.

Training and competency

Falls Prevention Policy

Supersedes the version effective 1 March 2025. Adds the falls lead nurse or therapist as a mandatory escalation contact, alongside the on-call registered manager, for any fall with suspected injury.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group assesses falls risk and responds when a resident falls. It applies to every resident, with particular attention to a resident identified as being at higher risk.

Policy statement

Falls prevention balances a resident's right to move around freely with a proportionate response to their individual risk, since an overly restrictive approach can itself cause harm by reducing a resident's mobility, confidence and independence.

Definitions

**Falls risk assessment** the structured assessment completed for every resident at admission and reviewed regularly thereafter. **Post-fall protocol** the immediate response steps followed after any fall, regardless of apparent severity. **Falls lead** the nurse or therapist now designated at each site as a mandatory escalation contact, alongside the on-call registered manager, for any fall with suspected injury.

Roles and responsibilities

**Care staff** follow the post-fall protocol immediately after any fall and contact the on-call registered manager, and now also the falls lead where injury is suspected. **The registered manager** reviews the falls risk assessment after any fall and updates the care plan accordingly. **The falls lead** provides a clinical assessment for any suspected-injury fall, a new role introduced in this version, working alongside the GP or emergency services where further escalation is needed.

Complete a falls risk assessment at admission and review it at least every three months, or sooner following any fall.

Following any fall, do not move the resident until a basic check for obvious injury has been completed, unless leaving them in place presents its own risk.

Contact the on-call registered manager immediately after any fall, regardless of whether an injury is apparent.

Equipment and property

A staff member issued a key, access card, uniform, device or other item of Alderbridge property is responsible for its reasonable care and safekeeping while in their possession, reporting a loss or damage promptly.

Extended worked example: a SAR received during active safeguarding involvement

A worked example illustrates a genuinely difficult overlap. A resident's family member submits a SAR while a safeguarding investigation involving that same family member is ongoing. Quality checking a response before it is sent

Before any SAR response is sent, a second person (not the person who prepared it) reviews it specifically for redaction completeness and factual accuracy, since a redaction mistake in a SAR response is itself a personal data breach under the Personal Data Breach Procedure, and this second check is a control specifically designed to prevent that particular failure mode.

Breach severity thresholds used for internal escalation

This procedure uses three internal severity bands to decide who is informed and how quickly, beyond the
regulatory notification decision itself: a low-severity breach (contained quickly, minimal data, no special
category information) is handled by the Data Protection Lead with a routine report to the next scheduled
compliance update; a medium-severity breach (special category data involved, or containment took longer

vulnerable individuals significantly affected, or a systemic cause suggesting other similar exposure may
exist) triggers immediate Chief Executive and Board Chair notification regardless of time of day.

Testing the breach response itself

The Data Protection Lead runs an occasional simulated breach scenario, similar in spirit to a fire drill, to
confirm the internal reporting chain and the Data Protection Lead's own investigation and notification
process work smoothly under realistic time pressure, rather than the process being tested for the first time
during a genuine, high-stakes incident.

Final note on why speed matters as much as thoroughness

A breach response that is eventually thorough but slow to start is far more damaging than one that starts
reporting and containing within minutes even if the full investigation takes longer to complete, since the
actual harm to an affected individual accumulates during every hour a breach remains uncontained, which
is precisely why this procedure's own internal reporting window is measured in a single hour rather than a
working day.

Coordinating with communications and reputation management

For any breach significant enough to carry a realistic risk of media or public attention, the Chief Executive
coordinates the organisation's external communications directly, ensuring the same honest,
plain-language standard described above for individual notification is maintained publicly too, rather than a
defensive public position being adopted that contradicts what affected individuals have themselves already

Safeguarding Training Levels: Who Needs What

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the different levels of safeguarding training required across Alderbridge roles. It applies to every member of staff and every registered manager.

Policy statement

Safeguarding training is matched to a role's actual level of resident contact and responsibility, so that every staff member holds the depth of training genuinely relevant to their duties.

Definitions

**Level 1** basic safeguarding awareness, required for every member of staff regardless of role. **Level 2** intermediate training for a role with direct, regular resident contact. **Level 3** advanced training for a registered manager, deputy, or designated Safeguarding Champion.

1. Complete Level 1 safeguarding awareness training as part of induction, regardless of role.
2. Complete Level 2 training within the first month for any role involving direct, regular resident contact.
3. Complete Level 3 training before taking on a registered manager, deputy, or Safeguarding Champion role.
4. Refresh the applicable level every three years, or sooner if guidance changes significantly.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the Adult Safeguarding Policy (the framework this training supports) and the Safeguarding Champion Role Guidance (governing the specific Level 3 role in more detail).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates level matching. A new administrative staff member with no direct resident contact completes Level 1 only, matching their actual role, while a new care assistant starting the same week completes both Level 1 and Level 2 within their first month, reflecting their direct resident contact.

sparse_candidates.chunk_text:
Statement. Race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation are each protected in recruitment, employment and care delivery alike, and a resident's own view is never used to justify discriminatory treatment of a member of staff on any of these grounds, even where the resident's view reflects a genuinely held but discriminatory personal belief.

Handling a resident's discriminatory request in practice

Where a resident expresses a discriminatory preference about who provides their care, the registered manager discusses this sensitively with the resident directly, explaining Alderbridge's position, and considers whether the underlying need behind the request (for example, a genuine same-sex-carer preference for intimate personal care, which is a legitimate dignity consideration) can be met without discriminating against staff on a protected characteristic; where the request is simply discriminatory with no such legitimate underlying need, it is not accommodated, and the conversation with the resident and, where relevant, their family is recorded in their care plan so the position is consistent across every shift and every member of staff involved in their care.

Appendix: reasonable adjustments in recruitment

This appendix illustrates common reasonable adjustments made during Alderbridge recruitment, for hiring managers unfamiliar with the range of what might be requested. A candidate with dyslexia may be given extra time for a written exercise, or the option to complete it verbally instead, agreed in advance rather than raised as a surprise on the day. A candidate with a hearing impairment may be offered a British Sign Language interpreter or a written transcript of interview questions in advance. A candidate with a mobility impairment is offered step-free interview access at every Alderbridge site, confirmed in the invitation itself rather than left for the candidate to ask about. A candidate managing a mental health condition may request a shorter interview with scheduled breaks. None of these adjustments are treated as exceptional accommodations requiring special justification once genuinely requested — hiring managers are trained to expect and normalise such requests as an ordinary part of running a fair process.

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. Self-neglect's formal addition in this version continues that same pattern.

The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. A self-neglect situation, in particular, calls empowerment and proportionality sharply into focus, since respecting a capacitous resident's own choice while still exercising a genuine duty of care requires balancing these principles carefully rather than defaulting reflexively to either extreme.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates self-neglect and the terminology alignment together. A resident with full capacity is declining support with personal hygiene to a degree affecting their skin health. The site Safeguarding Champion is consulted per the new Self-Neglect Guidance, working with the GP and multidisciplinary team to support the resident's own choice as far as possible while addressing the genuine health risk, and information about the situation is shared with the resident's GP per the multi-agency information sharing appendix's proportionality principle.

Frequently asked questions

**Does self-neglect override a resident's right to make their own choices?** No, the guidance is designed to respect a capacitous resident's autonomy while still offering support and monitoring a genuine health risk; it is not a route to override a lawful choice. **Why does the organisation still have two different safeguarding-titled roles?** The site-level Safeguarding Champion provides local, everyday expertise, while the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead oversees the whole suite and coordinates cross-site and multi-agency matters; the titles are now kept clearly distinct throughout this document.

Training and competency

Safeguarding training at every level introduces this overarching policy, its appendices, and the current Safeguarding Champion terminology, with the specific procedure relevant to a staff member's actual duties covered in more depth.

Monitoring and compliance

The organisation-level Safeguarding Lead reviews practice across the whole suite quarterly, including self-neglect cases and multi-agency information sharing decisions.

Record keeping and retention

Records for each specific safeguarding situation, including a self-neglect case and any information shared with an external agency, are retained per that situation's own procedure and the Records Retention Schedule.

Purpose and scope

This protocol sets out how Alderbridge Care Group works with external agencies to protect a resident from
harm, now explicitly including the agency routes relevant to a financial abuse concern. It applies to every
site and every member of staff.

Policy statement

A safeguarding concern is rarely resolved by Alderbridge acting alone; effective safeguarding depends on
genuine, well-coordinated partnership with external agencies, now explicitly including the Office of the

Definitions

multi-agency board. **Regional manager liaison role** the coordination function supporting a multi-site or

version, with statutory powers to investigate a concern about an attorney or deputy acting outside their
proper authority. **Action Fraud** the new external route, introduced in this version, for reporting a
suspected fraud against a resident.

Roles and responsibilities

Purpose and scope

Policy statement

A lone worker is issued a device with a panic button, GPS location and, for a newly issued device from this version onward, an automatic no-movement alert, paired with a mandatory check-in call and a now clearly defined escalation protocol if a check-in is missed.

Definitions

**Lone worker device** the issued device, now including an automatic no-movement (man-down) alert feature on a newly issued device. **No-movement alert** the new automatic feature, introduced in this version, alerting the monitoring service if the device detects no movement for a defined period, catching a situation where the wearer cannot press the panic button themselves. **Escalation protocol** the newly defined, staged response, introduced in this version, followed when an expected check-in call does not arrive.

A worked example illustrates a financial abuse concern, a category staff have told the Safeguarding Lead

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Wherever a resident is able to participate, their own wishes and views are sought and given real weight throughout a safeguarding process, not merely noted as a formality; this is especially central to a self-neglect situation, where the resident's own account of their choices and priorities is the starting point for any supportive response.

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Where a resident's safeguarding history involves a local authority area outside where their current Alderbridge site sits, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead liaises with the originating authority to ensure relevant history transfers appropriately, using the multi-agency information sharing principles this version formalises.

Learning from a serious case review

Where Alderbridge is involved in, or a sector-wide serious case review identifies a lesson relevant to, a serious safeguarding failure, the Safeguarding Lead ensures that lesson is considered against this overarching policy and its suite, with any resulting change tracked and communicated to staff.

Supporting a staff member involved in a difficult safeguarding case

A staff member closely involved in a distressing safeguarding case, whether as the person who raised the concern or as part of the response, is offered support similar to that available following a resident's death, recognising that safeguarding work, including a self-neglect case that can be particularly difficult to sit with, is emotionally demanding even when handled well.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy is the umbrella safeguarding document; several other documents govern specific
safeguarding-adjacent situations and are not restated here. The Allegations Against Staff Procedure
governs the parallel process that runs where the person alleged to have caused harm is a member of staff.
The Missing Person Procedure governs the specific immediate-search and police-contact steps where a
person supported cannot be located. The Mental Capacity Act Guidance Notes govern how capacity is
assessed for the specific decision at hand, referenced throughout this policy rather than duplicated. The
Resident Finances and Appointeeship Policy governs financial-abuse-adjacent concerns arising from how
a resident's own money is handled. The Whistleblowing Policy provides an alternative external route for a
member of staff who does not feel able to raise a concern through this policy's normal internal route.

Site-by-site implementation notes

Every Alderbridge site nominates a safeguarding champion (see the Safeguarding Champion Role
Guidance) as the first, informal point of contact for a member of staff unsure whether something is a
safeguarding concern, though this role never substitutes for the registered manager's own formal reporting
duty. Willow Bank Community Service's safeguarding champion additionally maintains a log of any
property-access concern raised by a community support worker (for example, a key safe code that
appears to have been shared beyond the people who should hold it), reflecting the specific risk profile of
lone community visiting rather than a residential setting.

Safeguarding Adults Board engagement

Alderbridge participates in the relevant local authority's Safeguarding Adults Board where a site's residents fall within that authority's area, contributing to multi-agency learning and receiving updates on local safeguarding priorities; the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead represents Alderbridge at this Board.

The role of an advocate

Where a resident lacks capacity to fully participate in a safeguarding process, or would benefit from independent support regardless of capacity, an independent advocate is arranged to represent the resident's own wishes and interests throughout the process, distinct from a family member's role.

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. Self-neglect's formal addition in this version continues that same pattern.

The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. A self-neglect situation, in particular, calls empowerment and proportionality sharply into focus, since respecting a capacitous resident's own choice while still exercising a genuine duty of care requires balancing these principles carefully rather than defaulting reflexively to either extreme.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates escalation in practice. A family member of a resident at Oakfield Lodge complains that visiting hours feel too restrictive. The registered manager's initial response explains the current arrangement but does not satisfy the family member, who escalates to the Quality Lead. The Quality Lead reviews the specific circumstances, finds no safeguarding or outbreak-related reason for the restriction the family member described, and agrees a change to the site's visiting arrangement — recorded as both a complaint outcome and a trigger to review the Visiting Arrangements Policy's wording for clarity, since the underlying confusion turned out to affect more than one family.

Frequently asked questions

**Will making a complaint affect the care my relative receives?** No — Alderbridge treats any suggestion of this extremely seriously; a complaint is never allowed to affect the standard of care provided, and any concern that it might have should be raised directly with the Quality Lead. **Can I complain anonymously?** Yes, though an anonymous complaint can be harder to investigate fully and a response cannot be sent back to an anonymous complainant. **What if my complaint is about the registered manager themselves?** It is raised directly with the Alderbridge Quality Lead rather than the registered manager being asked to investigate a complaint about themselves. **Is there a time limit for making a complaint?** There is no fixed cut-off, though a complaint about something that happened a long time ago may be harder to investigate fully, which will be explained transparently in the response.

Monitoring and compliance

Purpose and scope

Policy statement

Medication management at Alderbridge follows a consistent set of principles across every specific policy in this area, now including a formal severity classification for a medication incident and an escalation route aligned with the current safeguarding standard.

Definitions

**The medication policy suite** the full set of specific policies this overarching document signposts, including ordering, administration, self-administration, covert administration, PRN protocol, and homely remedies. **Medication incident severity** the new classification, introduced in this version, categorising a medication error or near miss by its actual or potential harm. **Safeguarding Lead-first escalation** the alignment introduced in this version, matching the Resident Finances and Appointeeship Policy's and the Safeguarding Policy (Overarching)'s current standard for a medication-related concern with a safeguarding dimension.

Roles and responsibilities

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds
or acting under a financial authority on a resident's behalf.

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Worked example

resident is sometimes specifically targeted by a scam or fraud, including one involving a caller
impersonating a trusted organisation; Action Fraud is the appropriate national reporting route for this kind

This policy works alongside the Duty of Candour Guidance, the Safeguarding Adults Policy, the Serious Incident Review Policy, and the CQC Notification Procedure, each of which governs a more specific aspect of what happens when something serious has gone wrong.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates escalation in practice. A family member of a resident at Oakfield Lodge complains that visiting hours feel too restrictive. The registered manager's initial response explains the current arrangement but does not satisfy the family member, who escalates to the Quality Lead. The Quality Lead reviews the specific circumstances, finds no safeguarding or outbreak-related reason for the restriction the family member described, and agrees a change to the site's visiting arrangement — recorded as both a complaint outcome and a trigger to review the Visiting Arrangements Policy's wording for clarity, since the underlying confusion turned out to affect more than one family.

Frequently asked questions

**Will making a complaint affect the care my relative receives?** No — Alderbridge treats any suggestion of this extremely seriously; a complaint is never allowed to affect the standard of care provided, and any concern that it might have should be raised directly with the Quality Lead. **Can I complain anonymously?** Yes, though an anonymous complaint can be harder to investigate fully and a response cannot be sent back to an anonymous complainant. **What if my complaint is about the registered manager themselves?** It is raised directly with the Alderbridge Quality Lead rather than the registered manager being asked to investigate a complaint about themselves. **Is there a time limit for making a complaint?** There is no fixed cut-off, though a complaint about something that happened a long time ago may be harder to investigate fully, which will be explained transparently in the response.

Training and competency

Registered managers and anyone likely to handle a complaint complete complaints-handling training, covering both this policy's process and the Duty of Candour Guidance.

Monitoring and compliance

Complaint themes, timescale compliance, and outcomes are reviewed at the quarterly Quality Committee, alongside compliments logged under the Compliments and Feedback Log, to give a balanced quality picture rather than a purely complaints-driven one.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds
or acting under a financial authority on a resident's behalf.

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. Self-neglect's formal addition in this version continues that same pattern.

The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. A self-neglect situation, in particular, calls empowerment and proportionality sharply into focus, since respecting a capacitous resident's own choice while still exercising a genuine duty of care requires balancing these principles carefully rather than defaulting reflexively to either extreme.

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Wherever a resident is able to participate, their own wishes and views are sought and given real weight throughout a safeguarding process, not merely noted as a formality; this is especially central to a self-neglect situation, where the resident's own account of their choices and priorities is the starting point for any supportive response.

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Where a resident's safeguarding history involves a local authority area outside where their current Alderbridge site sits, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead liaises with the originating authority to ensure relevant history transfers appropriately, using the multi-agency information sharing principles this version formalises.

Learning from a serious case review

Where Alderbridge is involved in, or a sector-wide serious case review identifies a lesson relevant to, a serious safeguarding failure, the Safeguarding Lead ensures that lesson is considered against this overarching policy and its suite, with any resulting change tracked and communicated to staff.

Supporting a staff member involved in a difficult safeguarding case

A staff member closely involved in a distressing safeguarding case, whether as the person who raised the concern or as part of the response, is offered support similar to that available following a resident's death, recognising that safeguarding work, including a self-neglect case that can be particularly difficult to sit with, is emotionally demanding even when handled well.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

Frequently asked questions

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds
or acting under a financial authority on a resident's behalf.

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. Self-neglect's formal addition in this version continues that same pattern.

The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. A self-neglect situation, in particular, calls empowerment and proportionality sharply into focus, since respecting a capacitous resident's own choice while still exercising a genuine duty of care requires balancing these principles carefully rather than defaulting reflexively to either extreme.

A worked example illustrates escalation in practice. A family member of a resident at Oakfield Lodge complains that visiting hours feel too restrictive. Frequently asked questions

**Will making a complaint affect the care my relative receives?** No — Alderbridge treats any suggestion of this extremely seriously; a complaint is never allowed to affect the standard of care provided, and any concern that it might have should be raised directly with the Quality Lead. **Can I complain anonymously?** Yes, though an anonymous complaint can be harder to investigate fully and a response cannot be sent back to an anonymous complainant. **What if my complaint is about the registered manager themselves?** It is raised directly with the Alderbridge Quality Lead rather than the registered manager being asked to investigate a complaint about themselves. **Is there a time limit for making a complaint?** There is no fixed cut-off, though a complaint about something that happened a long time ago may be harder to investigate fully, which will be explained transparently in the response.

Training and competency

Registered managers and anyone likely to handle a complaint complete complaints-handling training, covering both this policy's process and the Duty of Candour Guidance.

On a resident's death, their remaining personal allowance and any appointeeship-held funds are

Where a visitor gives a resident cash directly rather than through the site's own recording system, staff

since an unrecorded cash amount is one of the more common sources of an apparent discrepancy at the

Where a resident retains capacity to manage some or all of their own money, this is supported and

Transparent, well-recorded handling of resident money protects a vulnerable resident from a risk that can
otherwise go unnoticed for a long time, and routing a financial concern to the Safeguarding Lead in this
version exists to make sure that protection is treated with the urgency a safeguarding matter deserves.

Extended worked example: a financial concern

A worked example illustrates a financial abuse concern, a category staff have told the Safeguarding Lead
they find harder to recognise than physical harm. A care worker at Meadow Court notices that a resident's
small personal spending allowance, usually £20 a week and tracked in the individual resident finance
ledger under the Resident Finances and Appointeeship Policy, has been withdrawn in full every week for

resident can recall enjoying. The care worker does not confront the family member directly. Instead, the
concern is reported to the registered manager the same day, who reviews the ledger, finds no explanation
on file, and makes a safeguarding referral to the local authority, treating the pattern itself — not any single
withdrawal — as the trigger for concern, consistent with this policy's recognition that financial abuse is
often only visible as a pattern over time.

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Wherever a resident is able to participate, their own wishes and views are sought and given real weight throughout a safeguarding process, not merely noted as a formality; this is especially central to a self-neglect situation, where the resident's own account of their choices and priorities is the starting point for any supportive response.

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Where a resident's safeguarding history involves a local authority area outside where their current Alderbridge site sits, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead liaises with the originating authority to ensure relevant history transfers appropriately, using the multi-agency information sharing principles this version formalises.

Learning from a serious case review

Where Alderbridge is involved in, or a sector-wide serious case review identifies a lesson relevant to, a serious safeguarding failure, the Safeguarding Lead ensures that lesson is considered against this overarching policy and its suite, with any resulting change tracked and communicated to staff.

Supporting a staff member involved in a difficult safeguarding case

A staff member closely involved in a distressing safeguarding case, whether as the person who raised the concern or as part of the response, is offered support similar to that available following a resident's death, recognising that safeguarding work, including a self-neglect case that can be particularly difficult to sit with, is emotionally demanding even when handled well.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

Why the involvement description was expanded

Following the same CQC feedback that led the Statement of Purpose to strengthen its own service user involvement section, this guide is similarly updated so a resident and family reading this more accessible, everyday document also see the full picture of how they can genuinely shape the service, not only a brief mention of a residents' meeting, giving equal visibility to the involvement opportunities in whichever document a family happens to read first, at admission or at any later point.

Settling in during your first few weeks

Purpose and scope

This protocol sets out how Alderbridge Care Group works with external agencies to protect a resident from
harm, now explicitly including the agency routes relevant to a financial abuse concern. It applies to every
site and every member of staff.

Policy statement

A safeguarding concern is rarely resolved by Alderbridge acting alone; effective safeguarding depends on
genuine, well-coordinated partnership with external agencies, now explicitly including the Office of the
Public Guardian and Action Fraud for a financial abuse concern, aligning this protocol with the
Safeguarding Policy (Overarching)'s own formal recognition of financial abuse within its suite.

Definitions

**LADO** the Local Authority Designated Officer. **Safeguarding Adults Board (SAB)** the statutory
multi-agency board. **Regional manager liaison role** the coordination function supporting a multi-site or
complex concern. **Office of the Public Guardian** the new external agency route, introduced in this
version, with statutory powers to investigate a concern about an attorney or deputy acting outside their
proper authority. **Action Fraud** the new external route, introduced in this version, for reporting a
suspected fraud against a resident.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any member of staff** reports a safeguarding concern to the registered manager immediately. **The
registered manager** makes the initial external referral decision, now including a financial abuse concern's
specific new routes where relevant. **The organisation-level Safeguarding Lead** coordinates the most
complex situations, including a financial abuse concern requiring Office of the Public Guardian or Action
Fraud involvement, and attends the local Safeguarding Adults Board.

Frequently asked questions (further)

**What if the person doesn't want anything done about it?** Their wishes are taken seriously and inform
how the concern is handled, but the concern is still reported — a person's wish not to escalate a matter
does not remove the duty to report it, particularly where others might also be at risk from the same source.
**Can I be disciplined for raising a safeguarding concern that turns out to be unfounded?** No — provided
the concern was raised honestly and in good faith, raising it is never itself a disciplinary matter, even
where the investigation finds no abuse occurred. **What if the person causing harm is a visiting healthcare
professional, not an Alderbridge staff member or another resident?** The same reporting duty applies; the
registered manager additionally notifies that professional's own employer or regulatory body alongside the
local authority safeguarding team. **How quickly must I complete the Safeguarding Referral Form?** As
soon as possible and always the same day the concern is reported to the registered manager — it is never
left until the next scheduled admin time.

2. Listen to what you are told without interrupting, without promising confidentiality you cannot keep, and

Worked example

A worked example illustrates how a stock check discrepancy is handled in practice. At a routine evening
stock check at Oakfield Lodge, two staff find the physical tablet count for a controlled drug one short of the
register balance. Following this procedure, they do not simply adjust the register to match the physical
count. Instead, they report the discrepancy to the registered manager immediately, the cabinet is not
accessed again that shift beyond what is needed for any resident's own scheduled dose (administered
under full two-person witnessing as normal), and a Medication Error Report Form is raised recording the
exact discrepancy, the two staff who identified it, and every dose administered that day cross-checked
individually against the register to identify where the count diverges. In this example, the review finds that
an earlier administration that day was witnessed and given correctly but the second signature was, in
error, added to the wrong row of the register — a transcription error rather than a missing dose — and the
register is corrected by both original staff adding a dated, signed correction note next to the original entry,
never by erasing or overwriting the original entry itself.

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. Self-neglect's formal addition in this version continues that same pattern.

The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. A self-neglect situation, in particular, calls empowerment and proportionality sharply into focus, since respecting a capacitous resident's own choice while still exercising a genuine duty of care requires balancing these principles carefully rather than defaulting reflexively to either extreme.

Resident and family involvement in medication decisions

Wherever a resident has capacity, they are involved directly in decisions about their own medication; where capacity is lacking, family or an advocate is involved in a best-interests process rather than a purely clinical decision being made without any input beyond the care team itself.

Medication reconciliation on admission and transfer

Every resident's full medication list is reconciled against the prescribing GP's own record at admission, and again at any hospital transfer in either direction, since a mismatch between what a resident is believed to be taking and what they are actually prescribed is one of the most common sources of a serious medication error. This reconciliation is completed by a registered nurse or the registered manager, never left solely to an informal handover conversation.

Managing a medication change communicated verbally

Where a GP communicates a medication change verbally, this is confirmed in writing before the change is actually implemented, except in a genuine emergency where immediate action is clinically necessary; a verbal instruction alone is not treated as sufficient authority for an ongoing change to a resident's regular medication regimen.

End of life medication considerations

Medication management at the end of a resident's life often involves a different balance of priorities than routine administration, with comfort and symptom control given particular weight consistent with the End of Life Care Policy; this overarching document's core principles still apply in full, adapted to that different clinical context.

Safeguarding responsibilities

Closing note

This handbook is reviewed regularly to reflect current policy and legal requirements, and a staff member with a question about any benefit, term or policy it describes is encouraged to speak with their line manager, regional manager, or HR directly.

A resident at Oakfield Lodge is assessed as lacking capacity to manage her full financial affairs, but retains capacity to decide what she would like for lunch each day; staff continue to offer her genuine meal choices daily, never assuming the earlier, unrelated financial capacity finding extends to this entirely separate, everyday decision.

Frequently asked questions

**Who can carry out a capacity assessment?** Any appropriately trained member of staff for a routine decision; a more complex or contested decision may need input from a GP or other professional. **How often is a capacity assessment reviewed?** Whenever the decision needs to be made again, or if there is reason to believe the person's capacity may have changed, rather than treated as a permanent, one-off finding. **What if the family disagrees with a best interests decision?** Their view is a genuinely important part of the best interests checklist, but the final decision rests with whoever is legally responsible for making it, following the checklist properly and documenting how the family's view was considered.

Training and competency

All care-facing staff complete Mental Capacity Act training at induction and refresher training periodically, with more detailed training for staff regularly involved in best interests decisions.

Monitoring and compliance

The Safeguarding Lead reviews a sample of capacity assessments and best interests decisions quarterly for quality and correct application of the framework.

Record keeping and retention

Capacity assessments and best interests decisions are retained per the Records Retention Schedule, within the person's care file.

Appendix: categories of abuse in an Alderbridge context

This appendix expands on the Categories of Abuse section above with practical illustration for training
purposes. Physical abuse includes hitting, rough handling during personal care, or unnecessary restraint.
Sexual abuse includes any non-consensual sexual act or, for a person unable to consent, any sexual act
at all. Psychological abuse includes threats, humiliation, or deliberately isolating a person from friends and
family. Financial abuse includes theft, coercion over a will or property, or misuse of a person's benefits or
savings, and is often the hardest category to spot because it can look, superficially, like ordinary family
financial support. Neglect includes failure to provide adequate food, warmth, hygiene or medical attention.
Discriminatory abuse includes harassment or exclusion based on a protected characteristic.
Organisational abuse includes poor practice arising from the culture or systems of a whole service, not just
one individual's actions. Domestic abuse includes patterns of controlling, coercive or threatening
behaviour between people who are personally connected. Self-neglect includes a person's own inability or
unwillingness to meet their own basic needs, still treated as a genuine concern warranting a response, not
a lifestyle choice to be simply respected without further action.

Stock discrepancy investigation

Any stock discrepancy identified at a weekly count is investigated the same day by the registered manager, checking administration records first before considering whether an ordering or delivery error explains the gap, since most discrepancies trace back to a simple recording error rather than a genuine loss.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds
or acting under a financial authority on a resident's behalf.

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Purpose and scope

This protocol sets out how Alderbridge Care Group works with external agencies to protect a resident from
harm, now explicitly including the agency routes relevant to a financial abuse concern. It applies to every
site and every member of staff.

Policy statement

A safeguarding concern is rarely resolved by Alderbridge acting alone; effective safeguarding depends on
genuine, well-coordinated partnership with external agencies, now explicitly including the Office of the
Public Guardian and Action Fraud for a financial abuse concern, aligning this protocol with the
Safeguarding Policy (Overarching)'s own formal recognition of financial abuse within its suite.

Definitions

multi-agency board. **Regional manager liaison role** the coordination function supporting a multi-site or
complex concern. **Office of the Public Guardian** the new external agency route, introduced in this
version, with statutory powers to investigate a concern about an attorney or deputy acting outside their
proper authority. **Action Fraud** the new external route, introduced in this version, for reporting a
suspected fraud against a resident.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any member of staff** reports a safeguarding concern to the registered manager immediately. **The
registered manager** makes the initial external referral decision, now including a financial abuse concern's
specific new routes where relevant. **The organisation-level Safeguarding Lead** coordinates the most
complex situations, including a financial abuse concern requiring Office of the Public Guardian or Action
Fraud involvement, and attends the local Safeguarding Adults Board.

Safeguarding Training Levels: Who Needs What

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the different levels of safeguarding training required across Alderbridge roles. It applies to every member of staff and every registered manager.

Policy statement

Safeguarding training is matched to a role's actual level of resident contact and responsibility, so that every staff member holds the depth of training genuinely relevant to their duties.

Definitions

**Level 1** basic safeguarding awareness, required for every member of staff regardless of role. **Level 2** intermediate training for a role with direct, regular resident contact. **Level 3** advanced training for a registered manager, deputy, or designated Safeguarding Champion.

1. Complete Level 1 safeguarding awareness training as part of induction, regardless of role.
2. Complete Level 2 training within the first month for any role involving direct, regular resident contact.
3. Complete Level 3 training before taking on a registered manager, deputy, or Safeguarding Champion role.
4. Refresh the applicable level every three years, or sooner if guidance changes significantly.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the Adult Safeguarding Policy (the framework this training supports) and the Safeguarding Champion Role Guidance (governing the specific Level 3 role in more detail).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates level matching. A new administrative staff member with no direct resident contact completes Level 1 only, matching their actual role, while a new care assistant starting the same week completes both Level 1 and Level 2 within their first month, reflecting their direct resident contact.
